name: Tina Neill
highlight: Channel freestyle and backstroke successes · 2003 and 2005
biography: Tina Neill is an American swimmer and coach whose Channel career includes freestyle and backstroke crossings. An All-America swimmer at the University of California, Davis, she later coached age-group, high-school and college swimmers. Her Macalester College profile records work with the college and its Masters programme, as well as a Davis High School team recognised as mythical national champions in 1993.

Neill completed her first Channel attempt on 26 July 2003. Swimming from Samphire Hoe to Strouanne, she took 11 hours 21 minutes, supported by coach Bob Pearson and her sister Kathy Guinn. In a later interview, she explained that her interest in open water had grown from looking at a Minnesota lake and wondering whether she could swim its length.

Having raced backstroke and individual medley in college, she chose backstroke for a second Channel swim. On 9 August 2005 she reached Wissant in 13 hours 22 minutes. Guinness recognises that performance in its female backstroke category. Contemporary claims that she was the first person to cross using backstroke overlook Haydn Welch’s 1993 swim. Neill’s account describes navigating beside the escort boat and maintaining a backward-facing position during feeds, practical adaptations that distinguished this effort from her earlier freestyle crossing.

lines.text: CS&PF named historical record 443858 gives Tina Neill, USA/Minnesota, 26 July 2003, E–F, 11:21:00 and CSA attribution. Swimming World’s dated first-attempt account, opening two paragraphs, establishes departure and arrival on that day at 08:39 and 20:00 and an elapsed 11:21. Minute precision follows that narrative; no time zone is inferred. Neill’s later interview identifies the first crossing as freestyle.

lines.text: CS&PF historical record 443988 gives 9 August 2005, Tina Neill, USA/Minnesota, E–F, 13:22:00 and CSA attribution. Guinness’s named female-backstroke record agrees on date and 13:22. Swimming World supplies the stroke and landing account but its first-person assertion is not accepted: the later Neill interview’s backstroke chronology includes Haydn Welch in 1993. The dispute concerns the historical first claim, not the consistently reported time.
